rubric: States that timescales would be effectively short or memoryless
Explains that persistent states with longer memory would leave more non-zero coordinates than the roughly 20 active per token

items.question: Does the paper establish that long-timescale Persistent SAE features receive their new evidence mainly at punctuation and function words? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper motivates the possibility from work on contextual information in punctuation and structural markers, but says the direction and strength of any relationship are an empirical matter. It defines U_{q,c} for testing this without reporting such a conclusion.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the paper treats the direction of the relationship as empirical and only sets up the U_{q,c} analysis

items.question: Does the paper report that the Persistent SAE reconstructs hidden states better than BatchTopK in FVE? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper states that an extension should not degrade reconstruction and lists FVE and cosine similarity as metrics. Its text reports no comparative FVE values; Figure 4 shows only Persistent SAE training loss and state L0.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that FVE is set as a requirement or protocol metric but no comparison showing superiority is reported

items.question: Because the subject probing includes a supervised ranking, was the Persistent SAE exposed to MMLU subject labels in training? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The SAEs are trained only on Pile activations, and MMLU is never used for training. Labels enter only in the Eq. 8 score used to order features for the probe, computed after training as a reference point.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Explains that labels are used only post hoc for the supervised ordering or probe, while SAE training uses Pile data without labels

items.question: Does the AUC of 0.51 from the monitor's yes-minus-no logit show that Gemma-2-2B's layer-12 hidden states carry no information about the injection? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not supported. The 0.51 measures only the model's prompted answer. Whether the hidden states contain injection information is tested separately by the internal linear probes, which is exactly why the paper trains them rather than relying on prompting.
rubric: Answers that the claim is not supported (not settled or contradicted is acceptable, but not supported)
Explains that 0.51 concerns the prompted output, whereas internal information is assessed by separate probes on the hidden states

items.question: Can a Persistent SAE feature's state take negative values to encode evidence against the feature? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Both a(t) and h(t) are defined in the non-negative orthant. The state integrates non-negative sparse updates and is kept on the scale of those activations, so it cannot go negative.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Explains that a(t) and h(t) are non-negative by definition, since the state integrates non-negative activations

items.question: Does the matched setup ensure that the Temporal SAE reads exactly 2,048 hidden-state activations per step, like BatchTopK? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled, and likely not. The paper matches the number of reconstructed token positions per step, but the Temporal SAE's buffer returns previous–next pairs. It therefore also reads previous-token activations, and the paper says matching holds only up to the pairing its objective requires.
rubric: Answers not settled or not guaranteed
Explains that only reconstructed positions are matched, while pairs bring in extra previous-token activations

items.question: Is the supervised ranking guaranteed to be the best possible feature ordering for the linear probe at each budget? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not supported. It scores each feature independently by its mean-state difference for one subject, then interleaves the subjects round-robin. This ignores scale, variance and redundancy among features. The paper calls it a label-informed reference, not an optimal selection.
rubric: Answers that this is not supported or not guaranteed
Explains that the ranking uses per-feature mean differences (Eq. 8) with round-robin interleaving, which ignores variance and redundancy, so it is a reference rather than an optimum

items.question: Section 3 notes that a standard SAE might absorb the persistent part of the hidden state into its decoder bias. If that happened, would the feature-wise context correction experiment on that SAE reveal the persistence, and why?
items.answer: No. The correction only adds a learned multiple of each feature's own past activation along that feature's decoder direction. A constant bias is not tied to any feature's activation, so the correction would recover little error. The diagnostic would then indicate no feature-level temporal structure, even though the hidden states themselves are temporally correlated.
rubric: States that the correction would not reveal (or would barely reveal) the persistence.
Explains that the correction acts only through each feature's own past activation along its own decoder direction, and a bias term is not tied to any feature's activation.
Notes that hidden-state correlation can therefore exist without showing up at the feature level (or equivalent).

items.question: Suppose training drove about 60% of Persistent SAE features to the same memoryless timescale. Would differences in the relative update frequency U_{q,c} between the three lowest timescale quintiles reflect differences in timescale, and why?
items.answer: No. The quintiles are equal-sized splits by timescale, so the three lowest would all contain features with essentially identical (memoryless) timescales. How features are divided among those quintiles would be arbitrary with respect to timescale, so any U differences between them could not be attributed to timescale.
rubric: States that the differences would not reflect timescale.
Explains that equal-sized quintiles would place features with identical timescales into several quintiles, so the split between those quintiles is arbitrary.

items.question: Suppose one feature in a timescale quintile activates far more often than every other feature in that quintile. Would U_{q,c} for that quintile describe the token preferences of a typical feature in it, and why?
items.answer: Not reliably. Equation 4 pools all activation events of the quintile's features, conditioning on a_j>0 for any j in Q_q. The very frequent feature would contribute most of the events, so U_{q,c} would mostly reflect that one feature's token categories.
rubric: States that U_{q,c} would not reliably describe a typical feature.
Explains that Eq. 4 pools activation events over all features in the quintile, so a frequently firing feature contributes most events and dominates the ratio.

items.question: An analyst fits exponential decay curves to projection persistence for BatchTopK features using one minimum-activation-event threshold, and for Matryoshka features using a stricter threshold. Is a difference in fitted decay rates evidence that the two dictionaries differ in persistence, and why?
items.answer: No. Appendix D says fit parameters should be compared only between conditions measured under identical selection criteria. A different threshold changes which features and anchors enter each curve, so the difference in decay rates could come from the selection rather than from the dictionaries.
rubric: States that the difference is not valid evidence.
Explains that fitted parameters are comparable only under identical selection criteria, because different thresholds change which features and anchors contribute.

items.question: In the paper's dataset, benign trajectories also contain an untrusted span with benign content. Suppose instead that benign trajectories had no untrusted span at all. Would high probe accuracy at d=0 still indicate injection detection, and why?
items.answer: No. The d=0 checkpoint would then compare the end of a block of untrusted tool content against an ordinary position in a trajectory that has no such block. The probe could separate the classes on the mere presence of untrusted content rather than on the injection itself.
rubric: States that high accuracy would no longer indicate injection detection.
Explains that the probe could exploit the generic presence or absence of an untrusted span (structural difference) rather than injected instructions.

items.question: The Persistent SAE is trained on 256-token windows with the state reset each time, but it is run continuously over agent trajectories whose checkpoints lie much later than 256 tokens. Should its state scale drift into a regime never seen in training at those late positions, and why?
items.answer: Largely no. The contractive update with normalised new evidence keeps the state on the scale of the token-wise activations regardless of position. The hard cap makes every feature's memory finite, so the state depends mainly on recent tokens. This holds as long as effective memories are shorter than the 256-token training window.
rubric: States that the state should not drift (it stays bounded and comparable).
Cites stability (contractive update and normalised evidence) and finite memory from the hard cap as the reason.
Adds the condition that effective memories must be within the training window length, or equivalent.

items.question: Suppose a representation's injection probe spreads its coefficients almost evenly over several thousand features. Would its top-k=128 steering vector give a faithful test of whether the monitor uses the probed information, and why?
items.answer: Not fully. Taking only the top 128 features by absolute coefficient would capture just a small part of the probe direction. A weak steering effect could then reflect that truncation rather than the monitor ignoring the information. Comparisons with representations whose probe weights are concentrated would be biased against this one.
rubric: States that the test would not be faithful (it could understate the effect).
Explains that the top-128 restriction captures only a small fraction of a widely spread probe direction, so the effect depends on how concentrated the coefficients are.

items.question: Why does the paper standardise each representation separately before applying t-SNE with a single common hyperparameter setting?
items.answer: The compared representations differ greatly in scale and sparsity: dense raw hidden states, sparse BatchTopK features, the Temporal SAE's high-level group, and a subset of non-negative persistent states. With one shared perplexity and seed, unstandardised scale differences would change neighbourhood structure. The layouts would then reflect scale rather than subject organisation. Standardising puts the representations on a comparable footing.
rubric: Identifies that the representations differ in scale or sparsity (dense versus sparse versus state).
Explains that with shared t-SNE hyperparameters, scale differences would distort neighbourhoods, so standardising makes layouts comparable.

items.question: Why is taking the final 20 tokens of each MMLU sequence for the t-SNE analysis especially important for the Persistent SAE state?
items.answer: The persistent state starts at h(0)=0 and builds up evidence over tokens. Near the start of a sequence, long-timescale coordinates have accumulated little subject-specific evidence. By the final tokens, the state reflects substantial subject-specific preceding context.
rubric: Notes that the state starts at zero and accumulates evidence over the sequence.
Concludes that early tokens would underrepresent long-timescale subject information, whereas final tokens follow substantial subject-specific context.

items.question: Unlike the Temporal SAE, the Persistent SAE has no contrastive or smoothness term. What then pushes an individual feature toward a long timescale during training?
items.answer: Only the reconstruction objective on Eq. 3. A longer timescale is favoured when carrying a feature's past evidence forward along its decoder direction helps reconstruct later hidden states, that is, when the information the direction represents stays present in the residual stream. Otherwise the feature's timescale can stay short or become memoryless.
rubric: States that reconstruction loss alone drives the timescale.
Explains that a long timescale helps only when carrying the feature's past evidence along its decoder direction improves reconstruction of later hidden states.

items.question: In terms of the local versus global continuity distinction in Section 3, why might the Temporal SAE's temporal training signal mainly reward local continuity?
items.answer: Its buffer supplies adjacent previous–next token pairs, and its contrastive objective aligns high-level activations across neighbouring tokens. Consistency between adjacent tokens is exactly what local continuity, such as phrase continuation, produces on its own. Document-level context across sentences is therefore not directly targeted.
rubric: States that the signal mainly rewards local (adjacent-token) continuity.
Explains that training uses adjacent token pairs with a contrastive alignment of nearby tokens, which local phrase-level continuity alone can satisfy.

items.question: The paper does not filter trajectories by task utility. Why can the fixed injection probe still not learn the agent's later behaviour, such as task failure, as its cue for an injection?
items.answer: The probe is fit only at d=0, the final token of the untrusted span. The monitor model is causal, so its representation there depends only on tokens up to that point. The agent's later tool calls and outcomes are not yet visible, so the probe weights cannot be fitted to them.
rubric: States that the probe cannot learn later-behaviour cues during fitting.
Explains that fitting happens at d=0 and the causal monitor's representation there contains no information about later tokens or outcomes.

items.question: Why is the Persistent SAE's reconstruction fidelity measured from the persistent state h(t) via Eq. 3, rather than by decoding its token-wise activation a(t)?
items.answer: The decoder is trained to reconstruct from h(t). For long-timescale features, h carries evidence from earlier tokens that a(t) lacks. Decoding a(t) would evaluate a mapping the model was never trained for and would drop those carried contributions. The two agree only for memoryless features.
rubric: States that the decoder is trained to reconstruct from h, so fidelity must be measured from h.
Explains that a(t) omits evidence carried from earlier tokens by long-timescale features (the two coincide only when memoryless).

items.question: In spliced subject probing at very small feature fractions, why should the increasing-timescale ranking of the Persistent SAE state be expected to do poorly at most tokens?
items.answer: That ranking first selects near-memoryless features, whose state is essentially their sparse token-wise activation. Those features are zero except at the few tokens where they find evidence. With only a handful of them, most tokens give the probe all-zero inputs, so it has nothing to classify subject from.
rubric: States that this ranking should do poorly at small budgets.
Explains that the first-selected features are near-memoryless, so their state equals a sparse a(t) that is zero at most tokens.

items.question: At inference, if two different sequences happen to produce an identical hidden state x at some token, would the Persistent SAE's token-wise activations a(t) at that token be identical?
items.answer: Yes. With the thresholded form, a(t) is a deterministic function of the current hidden state alone. It does not depend on the SAE's previous state.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that a(t) is computed from the current hidden state only (thresholded encoder), independently of h(t-1).

items.question: At inference, if two different sequences happen to produce an identical hidden state x at some token, would the Persistent SAE's persistent states h(t) at that token be identical?
items.answer: Generally no. h(t) is computed from h(t-1) and a(t), so it depends on each sequence's earlier token-wise activations. Different histories give different states unless all features are memoryless.
rubric: Answers no (in general).
Explains that h(t) depends on the previous state and hence on the history of a, not only on the current hidden state.

items.question: Given that h(0)=0 at sequence start, would computing the fraction of alive features on the persistent state h instead of the token-wise activation a change which features count as alive?
items.answer: No. Each state coordinate is updated feature-wise from zero, so h_j becomes non-zero only after a_j has been positive at some token. A feature that never activates keeps a zero state, so the same set of features is alive under either view.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that with a zero initial state and a feature-wise update, h_j can be non-zero only if a_j was positive at some point.

items.question: If the initial state h(0) were a learned non-zero vector instead of zero, would computing the fraction of alive features on h instead of a change which features count as alive?
items.answer: Yes. A feature could then have a non-zero, decaying state from its initial value without its token-wise activation ever being positive. Measuring on h could make dead features look alive.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that a non-zero initial state lets h_j be non-zero even when a_j never activates, so dead features could appear alive.

items.question: In spliced subject probing at 100% of features, would the decreasing-timescale ranking give a different macro ROC AUC from the random rankings?
items.answer: No. At 100% every ranking hands the probe the same full set of state coordinates. Order no longer matters, and the curves should coincide.
rubric: Answers no (they coincide).
Explains that at the full budget all rankings include the same features, so the ordering is irrelevant.

items.question: In spliced subject probing at 0.1% of features, could the decreasing-timescale ranking give a different macro ROC AUC from the random rankings?
items.answer: Yes. At 0.1%, roughly 16 features are used, and different rankings select different subsets. The AUC can differ depending on whether timescale picks subject-relevant features.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that at a small budget the rankings select different small feature subsets (about 16 features), so performance can differ.

items.question: Under the fixed-probe protocol, representation A has accuracy 0.95 at d=0 and 0.70 at d=350, and representation B has 0.85 at d=0 and 0.83 at d=350. Which is better at local detection and which at retention?
items.answer: A is better at local detection, because detection concerns accuracy near d=0 and A scores 0.95 there. B is better at retention, because retention concerns how accuracy changes with distance: B loses 0.02 while A loses 0.25.
rubric: States that A is better at local detection and B is better at retention.
Justifies this by reading detection as accuracy near d=0 and retention as the change in accuracy with distance.

items.question: Adding a representation's steering vector with the positive sign raises the monitor's yes-minus-no margin by 0.6, and adding it with the negative sign raises the margin by 0.2. What direction-dependent effect remains after the paper's symmetric analysis?
items.answer: A direction-dependent difference of 0.4 (0.6 − 0.2), equivalently ±0.2 around a shared shift. The common +0.4 shift that both signs produce is a direction-independent effect of the perturbation, and the symmetric analysis removes it.
rubric: Gives a direction-dependent effect of 0.4 as the difference (or ±0.2 around a mean shift).
Identifies the shared positive shift (about +0.4) as a direction-independent perturbation effect that is removed.

items.question: How many features does each timescale quintile contain in the paper's 16,384-feature Persistent SAE, and how does that compare with the Temporal SAE's predefined high-level group?
items.answer: About 3,277 features (16,384/5 = 3,276.8). That is the same size as the Temporal SAE's 20% high-level group, so the longest-timescale quintile is a size-matched counterpart to that group.
rubric: Gives about 3,277 (3,276–3,277) features per quintile.
Notes that this equals the size of the Temporal SAE's 20% high-level group.

items.question: A team does not know in advance what fraction of a dictionary should carry contextual information. Based on the paper, should they choose a Temporal SAE or a Persistent SAE, and why?
items.answer: A Persistent SAE. A Temporal SAE requires fixing in advance a high-level subset that carries temporal information, such as the paper's 20%, which builds in experimenter bias. A Persistent SAE learns a timescale for every feature without any predefined partition.
rubric: Recommends the Persistent SAE.
Explains that the Temporal SAE requires a predefined high-level partition size, whereas the Persistent SAE learns per-feature timescales with no partition.

items.question: Could the paper's Pythia-160M Persistent SAE be used to build the monitoring representations in the AgentDojo case study? Why or why not?
items.answer: No. That SAE was trained on Pythia-160M's 768-dimensional layer-8 residual stream. The monitor reads Gemma-2-2B's 2,304-dimensional layer-12 residual stream. Its encoder and decoder directions do not apply there, so a Gemma-2-2B layer-12 SAE is required.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that the Pythia SAE is defined for a different model and layer (d=768, layer 8), whereas the monitor uses Gemma-2-2B layer 12 (d=2,304).

items.question: A team runs the feature-wise context correction on its own SAE. It finds gains above the unrelated-text control at a lag of 2 tokens, but no gains at lags of 50 tokens or more. What can they conclude about document-level context?
items.answer: Little. Short-lag gains are what local continuity, such as consecutive tokens of a phrase or sentence, produces. Evidence that features carry document-level context would require gains at long lags that exceed the unrelated-text control.
rubric: States that this does not show feature-level tracking of document-level context.
Explains that short-lag gains are consistent with local continuity, and global context would require long-lag gains beyond the control.

items.question: Under exact BatchTopK training with k=20, how many non-zero activation entries does a single Persistent SAE training step keep, compared with a flat-baseline step?
items.answer: The Persistent SAE keeps 20 × 2,040 = 40,800 entries per step, against 20 × 2,048 = 40,960 for the flat baselines. That is 160 fewer, while the average of 20 active features per token is the same.
rubric: Gives 40,800 for the Persistent SAE and 40,960 for the baselines (160 fewer).
Bases this on kB with 2,040 versus 2,048 tokens per step, keeping an average of 20 per token.

items.question: If the feature-wise context correction had found mostly negative per-feature parameters, which aspect of the Persistent SAE's design would the diagnostic fail to support?
items.answer: Its way of carrying information forward. The persistent state is non-negative and integrates past activations, so it adds a positive contribution along each feature's decoder direction. A negative parameter means past activation predicts a smaller contribution along that direction, which such a carried state cannot express.
rubric: Identifies the Persistent SAE's non-negative carried state (positive carry-forward along d_j) as unsupported.
Explains that negative parameters mean past activation predicts a reduced contribution along the same direction, which a non-negative accumulated state cannot represent.

items.question: If the Persistent SAE's state update mixed coordinates across features, which step of the monitoring case study's causal analysis could no longer be carried out as described?
items.answer: Building the steering vector. The paper weights the decoder directions of the features with the largest probe coefficients on h. That requires each state coordinate to correspond to one decoder direction. With mixing, probe weights on state coordinates would not map onto decoder columns, so the single-framework test of 'contains and is used' would break.
rubric: Identifies construction of the probe-weighted steering vector (the causal intervention) as broken.
Explains that it relies on each state coordinate being tied to a single decoder direction, which a mixing update would destroy.

items.question: If every Persistent SAE feature had learned the same non-memoryless timescale, which comparisons in the subject and token-category analyses would become uninformative?
items.answer: The timescale-versus-random comparison in spliced probing, the token-category analysis by timescale quintile, and the timescale-selected subsets. With identical timescales, ordering or splitting by timescale is arbitrary, so none of these could show whether timescales carry relevance.
rubric: Names the timescale-based rankings versus random (and/or the quintile analyses and timescale-selected subsets) as uninformative.
Explains that identical timescales make any ordering or grouping by timescale arbitrary.

items.question: If the hard cap limited every feature's effective memory to about 50 tokens, what could high fixed-probe accuracy of the long-timescale subset at d=200–350 no longer be attributed to?
items.answer: It could not be credited to the persistent state carrying the injection evidence forward from d=0. With roughly 50 tokens of memory, the d=0 evidence would have decayed by then. Any late accuracy would have to come from new evidence arriving in later tokens.
rubric: States that late accuracy could not be attributed to the state retaining evidence from the injected span.
Explains that a finite memory far shorter than the distance means the d=0 evidence would have decayed, so the signal must come from later tokens.

items.question: If the Persistent SAE had been trained with a dictionary four times wider than the baselines, which subject-probing comparison would become confounded, and why?
items.answer: The comparison of the Persistent SAE state with the baseline SAE representations at matched budgets. The same fraction of features would correspond to four times as many absolute features, and the model would have extra capacity. Any advantage could then reflect width rather than carrying state forward.
rubric: Identifies the Persistent-versus-baseline comparison at matched feature budgets as confounded.
Explains that unequal width changes absolute feature counts and capacity, so differences could come from width rather than persistence.

items.question: Does the k=128 restriction mean that the injection probes compared across representations use the same number of features? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The k=128 restriction applies only to building steering vectors. The logistic probes are fit on each full representation, for example the full Persistent state of 16,384 features versus the Temporal SAE's high-level group of about 3,277, so feature counts differ.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Explains that k=128 applies only to steering, and the probes use full representations of different sizes (for example 16,384 versus about 3,277).

items.question: Does the paper's setup guarantee that the Persistent SAE's token-wise activation a(t) has exactly 20 active features at every token? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. BatchTopK enforces k=20 as a batch-level budget, letting the number of active features vary across tokens, and the thresholded inference form also lets it vary per token. Twenty is the average, not a per-token count.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Explains that BatchTopK fixes only a batch-level (average) budget and the thresholded form lets per-token counts vary.

items.question: If the longest-timescale quintile had U above 1 for nouns, would that show that those features are mainly present at nouns? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. U_{q,c} is computed over positions where a_j>0, which is where new evidence arrives. For long-timescale features, the persistent state stays elevated across many later tokens. A noun preference describes where updates happen, not where the feature is present.
rubric: Answers contradicted (or not supported).
Explains that U counts token-wise update positions, while a long-timescale feature's state persists over subsequent tokens of any category.

items.question: If long-timescale features scored low on token-level autointerp but their states gave strong spliced subject probing, would the two results conflict? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted: the results would not conflict. Autointerp judges short windows of the token-wise activation, which fit long-timescale features poorly. The probing treats the persistent states jointly at the level of whole segments. A low local score does not imply that the features carry no meaningful information.
rubric: States that the results would not conflict.
Explains that autointerp uses short token-level windows ill-suited to long-timescale features, whereas probing evaluates joint state at segment level.

items.question: Does the case study show that Persistent SAE states retain the signal of every kind of indirect prompt injection attack in AgentDojo? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The positives are restricted to the important_instructions and direct attack types, and to failed attacks. Retention for other attack types was not evaluated.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that only important_instructions and direct attacks (with security=false) were used.

items.question: Does the paper establish that the learned timescales capture persistence in long-form fiction and subtitled dialogue? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Training uses Pile Uncopyrighted, which removes Books3, BookCorpus2, OpenSubtitles and YouTube Subtitles. The evaluations use Pile documents capped at 768 tokens, MMLU and AgentDojo, so neither book-length narrative nor subtitled dialogue is tested.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that the book and subtitle components were removed from the training data and that no evaluation covers such text.

items.question: If autointerp gave several long-timescale Persistent SAE features nearly identical descriptions such as 'academic text', would that show that those features are redundant? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper notes that features whose relevance is spread across a sequence may receive similar descriptions even when they are distinct, because the judge sees only short windows. Similar descriptions therefore do not establish redundancy.
rubric: Answers not settled (similar descriptions do not show redundancy).
Explains that token-level descriptions of distributed, long-timescale features can converge on broad domains even for distinct features.

items.question: In the Appendix D persistence measurement, suppose a feature's activation events cluster just after the 16-token prefix at the start of documents. Would a decline in its normalised projection at long lags be clean evidence that the feature's signal fades, and why?
items.answer: No. The long-lag points for these anchors fall at much later positions in the document, where hidden-state statistics differ. A decline could therefore reflect positional drift rather than fading of the feature's signal. Dropping the prefix and capping document length reduce this confound but do not remove it.
rubric: Concludes that the decline is not clean evidence of fading.
Explains that long lags from early anchors land at later positions whose hidden-state statistics differ (the positional-drift confound), and that the prefix drop and length cap only mitigate it.

items.question: Every trajectory ends with the same appended monitoring query. Would a representation that reflects only the current and immediately preceding tokens separate injected from benign trajectories at the final query position, and why?
items.answer: No. The local tokens at the query position are identical for both classes. Any separation there must come from information carried forward from earlier in the trajectory, so this checkpoint tests retention rather than local detection.
rubric: Concludes that a purely local representation would not separate the classes there (near chance).
Explains that the appended query text is the same for all trajectories, so only information carried from earlier can distinguish them.

items.question: Suppose the context correction's control replaced the past activations with zeros instead of past activations from unrelated text. Would a gain of the true-history correction over this control show that features carry document-specific history, and why?
items.answer: No. A zero control removes the marginal statistics of the activations. The true-history correction could then gain simply by adding a typical, bias-like activation level along each direction, without any document-specific relationship. The unrelated-text control keeps those marginals and removes only the link to the target document's history.
rubric: Concludes that the gain would not show document-specific history.
Explains that zeros discard the marginal activation statistics, so the gain could come from generic average-activation effects, whereas the unrelated-text control preserves those statistics.

items.question: Persistent SAE features are grouped by their own learned timescales, and smoothness is measured on the persistent state. If the longest-timescale group is smoother than the shortest, does that difference by itself show that the long group captures meaningful structure? Why?
items.answer: No. The grouping uses the same parameter that sets how strongly each state is smoothed over time, so the long group would be smoother by construction. This is why the paper calls the comparison asymmetric. Meaningfulness has to be checked with fidelity (FVE) and with independent evidence, such as projection-based persistence or subject information.
rubric: Concludes that the difference is not by itself evidence of meaningful structure.

Explains that the groups are defined by the timescale that controls smoothing of h, so greater smoothness follows by construction; independent checks such as FVE, projection persistence or probing are needed.

items.question: If each representation in the t-SNE comparison were projected with its own tuned perplexity rather than a common setting, would differences in how cleanly subjects cluster be comparable across representations, and why?
items.answer: No. t-SNE can exaggerate or suppress cluster separation depending on perplexity and initialisation. Tuning per representation would mix hyperparameter effects into the comparison, which is why the paper uses one perplexity and a fixed seed for all representations.
rubric: Concludes that the cluster differences would not be comparable.
Explains that t-SNE separation depends on perplexity and initialisation, so per-representation tuning confounds the comparison.

items.question: If the random-ranking reference in spliced subject probing were a single permutation rather than an average over several, would a gap between the decreasing-timescale curve and the random curve at the 0.1% fraction be reliable? Why?
items.answer: No. At 0.1%, only about 16 features are available, so the AUC depends heavily on which features one random draw happens to include. A single permutation is a high-variance reference, and averaging several permutations is what makes the comparison stable.
rubric: Concludes that the gap would not be reliable.
Explains that with very few features (about 16) a single random draw has high variance, and averaging over permutations is needed for a stable reference.

items.question: In the monitoring evaluation, why is the Persistent SAE's token-wise activation a(t) a particularly informative comparison for its state h(t), more so than the BatchTopK activations?
items.answer: a(t) and h(t) come from the same trained encoder and dictionary, and differ only in whether the state update has been applied. A difference in retention between them can therefore be attributed to carrying state forward. BatchTopK also differs in its training and in its learned dictionary.
rubric: States that a(t) and h(t) share the same encoder and dictionary, differing only by the state update.
Concludes that their difference isolates the effect of carrying state, unlike a comparison with a separately trained SAE.

items.question: Why does the relative update frequency U_{q,c} condition on a_j(t)>0 rather than on the persistent state h_j(t) being non-zero?
items.answer: The state is not sparse and stays non-zero for many tokens after evidence arrives, especially for long-timescale features. Conditioning on h would count tokens far from the update and mix the timescale itself into the statistic. a_j(t)>0 marks exactly the tokens where new evidence arrives, which is what the analysis is meant to measure.
rubric: States that h remains non-zero for many tokens after an update because it is not sparse, especially for long timescales.
Explains that a_j(t)>0 identifies where new evidence arrives, which is the quantity U is meant to characterise.

items.question: Why does the Persistent SAE's per-token inference cost grow only linearly with dictionary size, rather than quadratically as a general recurrent state over m coordinates might?
items.answer: The state update acts feature-wise. Each coordinate is updated only from its own previous value and its own token-wise activation, so a token requires m independent scalar updates. A dense recurrence would mix coordinates and need interactions among all m features.
rubric: Attributes the linear cost to the feature-wise update.
Explains that each coordinate depends only on its own past and activation, so there are m scalar updates rather than m-by-m cross-feature interactions.

items.question: In the causal analysis, why is the steering intervention applied at the final query token of a trajectory truncated at a later distance, rather than at the end of the injected span?
items.answer: The monitor's yes-minus-no margin is produced at the query token. Intervening there tests whether the direction affects the monitor's judgement at the moment it answers, after the delay that matters for long-context monitoring. Intervening at the span end would not test influence on the delayed decision.
rubric: States that the monitor's judgement (the yes-minus-no margin) is read out at the query token.
Explains that intervening there, after the chosen distance, tests causal influence on the delayed judgement rather than on local processing at the span.

items.question: Why does the paper describe a Persistent SAE as internalising the feature-wise context correction diagnostic?
items.answer: The correction adds a learned multiple of a feature's own past activation along its own decoder direction. A Persistent SAE's state likewise accumulates each feature's own past activations, decayed according to its timescale, and decodes them along that same direction. It does this across many lags and learns it jointly with the encoder and decoder during training, not post hoc on a frozen SAE.
rubric: Notes that both add a feature's own past activation along its own decoder direction, in the same feature-wise form.
Notes that the Persistent SAE does this across lags through its state and learns it jointly in training rather than post hoc.

items.question: Why are the BatchTopK, Matryoshka and Temporal SAE baselines probed with their full dictionaries rather than ranked by timescale like the Persistent SAE?
items.answer: The baselines have no per-feature timescale parameter, so an unsupervised ranking by timescale is undefined for them. Only the Persistent SAE exposes a timescale for every feature that can order its dictionary.
rubric: States that the baselines lack per-feature timescales.
Concludes that a timescale-based ranking cannot be built for them, so it applies only to the Persistent SAE.

items.question: Using the context correction preprocessing, roughly how many target positions in a document at the 768-token cap can be paired with a past activation at lag 10, compared with lag 700?
items.answer: After dropping the 16 prefix tokens, positions 16 to 767 remain, which is about 752. At lag 10, nearly all of them, about 740 to 750, have a valid past position. At lag 700, only about 50 to 70 do. Long-lag corrections therefore rest on an order of magnitude less data, and documents shorter than about 716 tokens contribute nothing at that lag.
rubric: Gives about 740–750 positions at lag 10 and about 50–70 at lag 700.
Explains that this follows from the 16-token prefix drop and the 768-token cap, so long-lag estimates use far fewer pairs.

items.question: In the monitoring case study, representation R has low fixed-probe accuracy at d=200, but adding its d=0 steering vector with opposite signs at d=200 produces a large, sign-dependent change in the monitor's margin. How should this be interpreted?
items.answer: R's direction appears to be used by the monitor's judgement even though it is only weakly decodable at that position. The paper explicitly allows this case, since decodability and causal use can come apart. The symmetric design rules out a generic perturbation effect.
rubric: Concludes that the direction influences the monitor despite weak decodability.
Explains that probe accuracy and causal use can diverge, and that the sign-dependent difference excludes direction-independent effects.

items.question: A team scales the Persistent SAE dictionary from 16,384 to 65,536 features. How does the per-token cost of the state update change, and does it depend on how long the trajectory is?
items.answer: The per-token cost grows about fourfold, because the cost is linear in dictionary size. It does not depend on trajectory length, because the state is updated once per token online.
rubric: States that the per-token update cost grows about 4×.
States that it is independent of sequence length, because the update is linear in m and done once per token from the previous state.

items.question: A team replicating the spliced probing gives each sequence three abstract-algebra segments for every one segment of each other subject. Which control in the paper's design have they lost, and what risk does it introduce?
items.answer: They have lost the within-sequence balancing that makes each subject's prior uniform. A probe could then improve its score partly by favouring the frequent subject rather than by tracking the current subject.
rubric: Identifies the loss of subject balancing (a uniform prior).
Explains the risk that the probe exploits subject frequency instead of tracking the current subject.

items.question: Over its full training run, how many separate 256-token windows does the Persistent SAE process, each starting from a reset state?
items.answer: About 1.95 million windows: 8 windows per step × 244,140 steps = 1,953,120. Each starts with h(0)=0, including later windows of long documents, which are treated as fresh sequences.
rubric: Gives about 1,953,120 (about 1.95M) windows.
Bases this on 8 sequences per step over 244,140 steps, each with its state reset.

items.question: In the steering analysis, what fraction of the available features does the k=128 steering vector use for the Temporal SAE's high-level group, compared with the Persistent SAE's full state?
items.answer: The Temporal high-level group has about 3,277 features (20% of 16,384), so 128 is about 3.9% of it. For the full Persistent state, 128 of 16,384 is about 0.8%. The absolute number of features is matched, but the fraction of each representation's pool is not.
rubric: Gives about 3.9% for the Temporal high-level group and about 0.8% for the full Persistent state.
Uses the 20% partition (about 3,277 features) and m=16,384, noting that the count is matched but the fraction differs.

items.question: If the Persistent SAE's token-wise activation a(t) had retained the injection signal across distance as well as its state h(t) did, which conclusion would lose support?
items.answer: The attribution of the Persistent SAE's retention to its persistent state would lose support. If the un-integrated activations retain the signal equally well, the state update adds nothing for long-context monitoring.
rubric: Identifies the conclusion that the carried state is responsible for retention.
Explains that the same encoder without the state update would perform equally, so the state adds no retention benefit.

items.question: If the decreasing-timescale ranking had matched the supervised ranking's macro ROC AUC at every feature fraction, what would that imply about the paper's aim of an unsupervised context summary?
items.answer: The unsupervised timescale criterion would be selecting subject-relevant features as well as the label-informed upper reference. A compact, inspectable subject summary could then be obtained without labels.
rubric: Concludes that the gap to the label-informed reference would be essentially zero.
Explains that timescale alone would suffice to pick a compact subject summary without supervision.

items.question: If the long-timescale Persistent SAE subset had high fixed-probe accuracy at late distances but its symmetric steering produced no direction-dependent change in the monitor's margin, which claim would lose support?
items.answer: The claim that this representation is used by the monitor's judgement, as opposed to merely containing injection information, would lose support. The probe could be exploiting directions that the model itself does not use.
rubric: Identifies the claim that the representation is used for (causally influences) the monitor's judgement.
Explains that probe accuracy alone shows containment, which can rest on directions the model does not use.

items.question: Suppose a dense linear map from past activations to the current hidden state recovered substantial reconstruction error, but the feature-wise context correction recovered none beyond the unrelated-text control. What would that imply for the motivation behind Persistent SAEs?
items.answer: It would weaken the motivation. The dense gain would reflect only the known correlation between consecutive hidden states. The null feature-wise result would indicate that individual standard-SAE features do not carry reconstruction-relevant information forward along their own directions.
rubric: Concludes that the motivation for feature-level persistence would weaken.
Explains that the dense gain is attributable to hidden-state correlation, whereas only the feature-wise result speaks to individual features.

items.question: If every representation, including the raw hidden state, had been near chance at d=0, which part of the monitoring analysis would lose its basis?
items.answer: The retention analysis would lose its basis. The probe is fitted at d=0, so with no local detection there would be no signal whose persistence could be measured at later distances. The steering directions, also built at d=0, would be uninformative too.
rubric: Identifies the retention, or fixed-probe distance, analysis as losing its basis (steering may also be mentioned).
Explains that both depend on a probe or direction fitted at d=0, which would carry no signal.

items.question: If the Matryoshka SAE's predefined high-level group had been as smooth as the Temporal SAE's high-level group, what would that suggest about the Temporal SAE's contrastive objective?
items.answer: Its smoothness could not be credited to the contrastive temporal objective. Matryoshka uses the same 20%/80% partition without any temporal signal, so the partition or nesting alone would account for the smoothness.
rubric: Concludes that the contrastive objective would add little to smoothness.
Explains that Matryoshka shares the partition but has no temporal training signal, so it serves as a control.

items.question: Does the finding of Lubana et al. that past hidden states explain much of the current hidden state establish that standard SAE features carry temporal information? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper argues that hidden-state correlation does not imply feature-level persistence. A sparse decomposition may spread the persistent part across many features or absorb it into a bias term or into features that fire on almost every token, so the question is empirical and concerns the decomposition.
rubric: Answers not settled (it does not establish it).

Explains that hidden-state correlation can be absorbed by the decomposition (spread across features, absorbed into the bias or into ubiquitous features), so feature-level persistence is a separate empirical question.

items.question: Does a large direction-dependent steering effect on the monitor's yes-minus-no margin show that the monitor would then correctly flag injected trajectories? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The steering analysis measures changes in the margin, which show causal influence. Prompting the monitor alone yields AUC 0.51, and the paper evaluates no steered classification accuracy, so it does not show that steering makes the monitor flag correctly.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the analysis measures margin changes (causal influence), not flagging accuracy, and that the monitor's own answers are near chance (AUC 0.51).

items.question: If the feature-wise context correction showed clear gains on a frozen BatchTopK SAE, would that establish that a Persistent SAE trained under matched settings outperforms BatchTopK? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper frames the two as answering distinct questions. The correction asks whether an atemporal decomposition leaves feature-level temporal information unused. A Persistent SAE learns a different decomposition jointly, so its outcome is not determined by the post-hoc result.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the post-hoc diagnostic and joint training answer different questions, so a positive diagnostic does not guarantee the trained model's performance.

items.question: Does the matched training setup mean the Persistent SAE has exactly the same number of learned parameters as the BatchTopK SAE? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The setup matches width, sparsity, optimiser, steps and token budget, but the Persistent SAE additionally learns a timescale parameter for every feature. That adds about 16,384 parameters, which is small relative to the encoder and decoder.
rubric: Answers contradicted (not exactly equal).
Explains that the Persistent SAE adds a per-feature timescale parameter (about m=16,384 extra), while the matched quantities do not include parameter count.

items.question: Does the matched setup ensure that the Persistent SAE sees activations from as many distinct documents per step as the flat baselines? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not supported. The setup matches activation tokens per step, not documents. Each Persistent SAE step draws 8 contiguous 255-token windows, so about 8 documents, whereas the flat baselines draw shuffled tokens from a mixture of many documents. Per-step document diversity is therefore lower for the Persistent SAE.
rubric: Answers that this is not ensured (contradicted or not settled, with per-step diversity likely lower).
Explains that tokens, not documents, are matched, and that the Persistent SAE uses 8 windows per step while the flat baselines mix shuffled tokens from many documents.

items.question: Does the paper show that long-timescale Persistent SAE states track subject in ordinary Pile documents, beyond MMLU? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The subject analyses (t-SNE and spliced probing) use only five MMLU subjects. Pile is used for training and for temporal statistics, not for subject probing.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that subject evidence comes only from five MMLU subjects, with no subject evaluation on Pile.

items.question: Under the fixed d=0 probe protocol, suppose a representation encodes the injection along the same direction at every checkpoint. Would its probe accuracy be expected to drop with distance because of how it encodes the signal?
items.answer: No. A fixed probe transfers when the encoding direction is stable, so this representation's accuracy would not drop because of drift.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that a stable encoding direction lets the d=0 probe keep working at later checkpoints.

items.question: Under the fixed d=0 probe protocol, suppose a representation encodes the injection at every checkpoint, but along a direction that rotates with distance. Would its probe accuracy be expected to drop with distance because of how it encodes the signal?
items.answer: Yes. The probe was fitted to the d=0 direction and is not retrained, so drift in the encoding lowers accuracy even though the information is present. This is exactly what the fixed protocol is designed to expose.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that the probe is not retrained, so a drifting encoding defeats it even when the information remains present.

items.question: In the autointerp pipeline, if scoring used held-out contexts disjoint from those shown during explanation, would a high score reward memorisation of specific examples?
items.answer: No. With disjoint held-out contexts, a high score requires the explanation to generalise to new inputs.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that held-out scoring contexts require generalisation beyond the explained examples.

items.question: In the autointerp pipeline, if scoring reused the same contexts that were shown during explanation, would a high score reward memorisation of specific examples?
items.answer: Yes. The judge could predict activations from having seen those exact examples, so the score would reflect memorisation rather than a generalisable description.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that reused contexts let the score come from recalling the specific examples rather than from generalisation.

items.question: In the Appendix D persistence analysis, if a feature with clearly positive elevation at its activating tokens and plenty of valid anchors were included, would its normalised persistence measure be stable?
items.answer: Yes. Normalising by a clearly non-zero elevation at the activating token gives a well-defined, stable measure.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that the normalising denominator (the elevation at the activating token) is clearly non-zero.

items.question: In the Appendix D persistence analysis, if a near-dead feature with near-zero elevation at its activating tokens were included by adding a small constant to the denominator, would its normalised persistence measure be stable?
items.answer: No. With a near-zero denominator, the regularised ratio can become arbitrarily large or unstable, which is why the paper excludes such features rather than regularising them.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that a near-zero elevation makes the ratio blow up or become unstable even with a small added constant.

items.question: After a standard SAE feature activates, suppose its signal lingers in the hidden state but stays below the encoder's sparsity threshold. Would tracking the sparse activation f_j at later tokens reveal the lingering signal?
items.answer: No. f_j is zero whenever the feature is below the sparsity threshold, so the sub-threshold signal is invisible in the sparse activation.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that the sparse activation is zeroed below the threshold.

items.question: After a standard SAE feature activates, suppose its signal lingers in the hidden state but stays below the encoder's sparsity threshold. Would tracking the projection p_j=d_j^T x at later tokens reveal the lingering signal?
items.answer: Yes. The projection is defined at every token, so it can reveal signal that is present but not selected by the encoder. It remains subject to the confound from correlated, non-orthogonal decoder directions.
rubric: Answers yes (possibly with the correlated-direction caveat).
Explains that the projection is defined at every token regardless of the sparsity threshold.

items.question: In the steering analysis, if one representation's top-128 probe coefficients were all 10 times larger than another's, would its steering vector at the same intervention position have a larger norm?
items.answer: No. The probe-weighted direction is normalised and rescaled to ρ=0.1 of the hidden-state norm, so the overall scale of the coefficients does not affect its magnitude.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that the direction is normalised and scaled to a fixed fraction of the hidden-state norm.

items.question: In the steering analysis, if the hidden-state norm at one intervention position were 10 times larger than at another, would the steering vector applied there have a larger norm?
items.answer: Yes. Its norm is set to ρ=0.1 of the hidden-state norm at the intervention position, so it would be 10 times larger.
rubric: Answers yes (about 10× larger).
Explains that the norm is defined as a fixed fraction ρ=0.1 of the local hidden-state norm.
